title: Spheres, cylinders and unduloids are the commonest unicellular forms

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Spheres, cylinders and unduloids are the commonest unicellular forms

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Of the six surfaces of revolution with constant mean curvature (plane, sphere, cylinder, catenoid, unduloid, nodoid), spheres, cylinders and unduloids are the commonest forms of small unicellular organisms and of cells in simple aggregates, and transitions between them are frequent during growth, reproduction and development.

fields.label: Notation
fields.value: 1/r_1 + 1/r_2 = \text{const}; surfaces of revolution: plane, sphere, cylinder, catenoid, unduloid, nodoid

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. V: The Forms of Cells

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: That spheres, cylinders and unduloids are of the commonest occurrence among the forms of small unicellular organism, or of individual cells in the simpler aggregates, and that in the processes of growth, reproduction and development transitions are frequent from one of these forms to another, is obvious to the naturalist

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter V, “The Forms of Cells”; topic “Plateau's surfaces of revolution in cells”. Scope: unicellular organisms and cells of simple aggregates

fields.label: Notation
fields.value: 1/r_1 + 1/r_2 = \text{const}; surfaces of revolution: plane, sphere, cylinder, catenoid, unduloid, nodoid

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch05-10: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.62

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The six candidate geometries permit explicit model selection. Existing images can test selected taxa and dynamics, but biased coverage prevents a reliable estimate of what is commonest across the stated scope.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Segment representative unicellular organisms and aggregate cells in 3D, fit all six constant-mean-curvature surface families, and estimate their frequencies and transitions in time-lapse sequences. The claim is supported if sphere, cylinder, and unduloid fits dominate and transitions among them are common.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Many images are 2D projections.

A threshold for classifying approximate surface families is needed.

Repository sampling is not representative of unicellular diversity.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data adequacy: 0.4
discriminating power: 0.7
analysis feasibility: 0.5
operationalizability: 0.8
data existence: 0.65

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The six-way classification is well defined, and bacterial shape compilations already separate spheres and cylinders at large sample size. Unduloids and the protists where Thompson saw them are poorly coded, and developmental transitions are not in the tables. A frequency ranking is therefore available for a biased subset, not for unicells in general.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Classify outlines of unicells and cells in simple aggregates as plane, sphere, cylinder, catenoid, unduloid or nodoid, and test whether spheres, cylinders and unduloids are the most frequent, including during growth and division. That frequency ranking would support the claim; a ranking led by other families, or by irregular outlines, would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Bacterial vocabularies collapse unduloids into rods or spirals.

Transitions during growth need time series, which these archives mostly lack.

Protist coverage in open shape tables is much thinner than bacterial coverage.
